source_text: Putatis autem nos occultare quod colimus, si delubra et aras non habemus? Quod enim simulacrum Deo fingam, quum, si recte existimes, sit Dei homo ipse simulacrum? Templum quod ei exstruam, quum totus hic mundus, ejus opere fabricatus, eum capere non possit? et, quum homo latius maneam, intra unam aediculam vim tantae majestatis includam? Nonne melius in nostra dedicandus est mente, in nostro imo consecrandus est pectore? Hostias et victimas Domino offeram, quas in usum mei protulit, ut rejiciam ei suum munus? ingratum est; quum sit litabilis hostia bonus animus, et pura mens, et sincera sententia. Igitur, qui innocentiam colit, Domino48 supplicat; qui justitiam, Deo libat; qui fraudibus abstinet, propitiat Deum; qui hominem periculo surripit, optimam victimam caedit. Haec nostra sacrificia, haec Dei sacra sunt; sic apud nos religiosior est ille qui justior. At enim, quem colimus Deum, nec ostendimus nec videmus: immo ex hoc Deum credimus, quod eum sentire possumus, videre non possumus. In operibus enim ejus et in mundi omnibus motibus virtutem ejus semper praesentem aspicimus, quum tonat, fulgurat, fulminat, quum serenat. Nec mireris si Deum non videas: vento et flatibus omnia impelluntur, vibrantur, agitantur; et sub oculos tamen non venit ventus et flatus. In sole adeo, qui videndi omnibus causa est, videre non possumus; radiis acies submovetur, obtutus intuentis hebetatur: et, si diutius inspicias, omnis visus exstinguitur. Quid? ipsum solis artificem, illum luminis fontem possis sustinere, quum te ab ejus fulgoribus avertas, a fulminibus abscondas? Deum oculis carnalibus vis videre, quum ipsam animam tuam, qua vivificaris et loqueris, nec aspicere possis, nec tenere? (XVII) Sed enim Deus actum hominis ignorat, et, in coelo constitutus, non potest, aut omnes obire, aut singulos nosse. Erras, o homo, et falleris. Unde enim Deus longe est, quum omnia coelestia terrenaque, et quae extra istam orbis provinciam sunt, Deo cognita, plena sint? Ubique non tantum nobis proximus, sed infusus est. In sole adeo rursus intende: coelo adfixus, sed terris omnibus sparsus est; pariter praesens ubique interest et miscetur omnibus, nusquam enim claritudo violatur. Quanto magis Deus, auctor omnium ac speculator omnium, a quo nullum potest esse secretum, tenebris interest, interest cogitationibus nostris quasi alteris tenebris. Non tantum sub illo agimus, sed et cum illo, ut prope dixerim, vivimus.
pass_a_gloss: You think that we hide what we worship, if we do not have temples and altars? For what image of God shall I fashion, since, if you think correctly, man himself is the image of God? What temple shall I build for Him, since the whole world, made by His work, cannot contain Him? And, since man remains wider, shall I enclose the power of such greatness within one small shrine? Is it not better that He be dedicated in our mind, consecrated in our innermost heart? Shall I offer sacrifices and victims to the Lord, which He has provided for my use, so that I may reject His gift? It is ungrateful; for a pleasing sacrifice is a good soul, and a pure mind, and a sincere sentiment. Therefore, he who cultivates innocence supplicates the Lord; he who cultivates justice makes a libation to God; he who abstains from frauds propitiates God; he who snatches a man from danger sacrifices the best victim. These are our sacrifices, these are the sacred rites of God; thus, among us, he who is more just is more religious. But, you say, the God we worship, we neither show nor see: indeed, we believe God because of this, that we can perceive Him, but we cannot see Him. For in His works and in all the movements of the world, we always behold His power present, when it thunders, flashes, and lightnings, when it clears. Do not be surprised if you do not see God: everything is driven, vibrated, and agitated by the wind and breezes; and yet, the wind and breeze do not come before our eyes. Even in the sun, which is the cause of sight for all, we cannot see; our vision is removed by its rays, the gaze of the beholder is dulled: and if you look longer, all sight is extinguished. What? Can you endure the craftsman of the sun, the fountain of light, when you turn away from its splendors, and hide from its lightnings? You want to see God with carnal eyes, when you cannot even see your own soul, by which you are vivified and speak? But, you say, God is ignorant of man's actions, and, established in heaven, cannot either visit all or know individuals. You err, O man, and are deceived. For where is God far, when all celestial and terrestrial things, and those outside this world's province, are known and full of God? He is not only near to us everywhere, but also infused. Consider the sun again: fixed in the sky, but spread throughout all lands; equally present everywhere, it is concerned with and mixed with all things, for its clarity is nowhere violated. How much more so God, the author and spectator of all things, from whom no secret can be hidden, is concerned with our darkness, and is concerned with our thoughts as if with other darknesses. We do not only act under Him, but also, as I might say, live with Him.
pass_b_english: Do you imagine we conceal the object of our worship simply because we lack temples and altars? What image of God could I fashion when, if you think rightly, humanity itself is the image of God? What temple could I build for Him when the entire world, created by His hand, cannot contain Him? And since a human being exceeds any single structure, would I enclose such greatness within one small shrine? Is it not far better that He be dedicated in our minds and consecrated in our inmost hearts? Should I offer sacrifices and victims to the Lord — gifts He provided for my own use — only to reject His own gift? That would be ingratitude; for the acceptable sacrifice is a good soul, a pure mind, and a sincere disposition. Therefore, the one who cultivates innocence supplicates the Lord; the one who cultivates justice pours out a libation to God; the one who abstains from fraud propitiates God; the one who snatches a person from danger slaughters the finest victim. These are our sacrifices; these are God's sacred rites. Consequently, among us the more just a person is, the more religious they are.

You object that we neither show nor see the God we worship. Precisely because we can perceive Him yet cannot see Him, we believe He is God. In His works and in every movement of the world we constantly behold His power present — when it thunders, flashes, lightens, and when the sky clears. Do not be surprised that you do not see God: wind and breezes drive, vibrate, and agitate everything, yet the wind itself never comes before our eyes. Even the sun, the very cause of sight for all, cannot be looked at; its rays push back our vision and dull the gaze of the beholder, and if you stare longer, all sight is extinguished. So can you endure the craftsman of the sun, the fountain of light, when you turn away from its splendor and hide from its lightning? You demand to see God with carnal eyes when you cannot even see your own soul, the very principle by which you live and speak?

You claim God is ignorant of human actions and, enthroned in heaven, cannot visit all or know individuals. You are mistaken, O man, and deceived. How could God be distant when all things celestial and terrestrial, and those beyond this world's sphere, are known to Him and filled with Him? He is not merely near us everywhere; He is infused throughout. Consider the sun again: fixed in the sky, yet spread over all lands; equally present everywhere, it engages and mingles with all things, for its clarity is nowhere violated. How much more, then, does God — author of all and spectator of all, from whom no secret can be hidden — penetrate our darkness and engage our thoughts as if they were another darkness. We do not merely act under Him; we live with Him, as it were.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the theological nuances and agency of the original. All arguments, including the analogies of the wind and the sun, are preserved.
